newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian crisis sends stock markets into tailspin.
newsitem.headline: Indian crisis sends stock markets into tailspin.

text.p: A political crisis ripped through Indian stocks on Monday, tearing more than eight percent off Bombay's benchmark index as investors watched the government struggle to face a challenge from a former ally, analysts said.
"It's certainly an unpalatable turn of events," said Bharat Iyer, strategist at UBS Securities. "It's very confusing."
Share prices went into a tailspin on Sunday's news that the the Congress party had withdrawn its make-or-break support to Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's 10-month-old government.
By noon (0630 GMT) on Monday, Bombay's benchmark stocks index was down 241.43 points, or 6.7 percent, at 3422.10 -- after plummetting more than 8.0 percent in early trade.
"Every time a politician says something in the coming weeks, the market will move sharply," Iyer said. "It's going to be a traders nightmare."
Analysts said they were advising institutional investors to keep a low profile until the political picture cleared.
"We're telling investors to wait-and-watch rather than sell right into the panic," said Bidisha Ganguly, economist at W.I. Carr Securities.

"We believe that in the short-term investors shouldn't sell into the vacuum. They should look for a buying opportunity at around 3100 points," said Robert Jackson, chief dealer at Jardine Fleming India Broking.
Analysts said it was unclear how Congress, which has only 140 deputies in the 545-seat Lok Sabha, or lower house, could form a government.
"Everyone's confused about what Congress gets out of this move," said Keshav Sanghi, salesman at James Capel B&K in Hong Kong. "Investors are fed up."

Analysts said the surprise move -- which came just days after the government raised international equity of more than $500 million in telecommunications firm Videsh Sanchar Nigam Ltd (VSNL) -- would hit plans to sell equity in other state-run firms.
"Consider the rest of the divestment programme shot at least for the next six months," Capel B&K's Sanghi said.
Analysts said the Congress decision was bound to affect budget proposals, announced by the United Front last month.

In the annual budget for 1997/98 (April-March), Finance Minister P. Chidambaram announced sweeping cuts in corporate and personal taxes. The proposals are scheduled to be passed by parliament once it reconvenes on April 21.
"One big question mark now is the budget," said W.I. Carr's Ganguly.
Some analysts said Chidambaram's Tamil Maanila Congress would probably support the Congress in its bid for power only if there were no significant changes in the budget proposals.
"We don't think the Congress, if it comes to power, will change the budget significantly," said a chief dealer at a foreign brokerage.
